spots.name: Hogan Butte Nature Park (Volcanic Viewpoint)
spots.tip: The summit lawn of this extinct volcanic vent (about 930 ft) is the best easy Mt. Hood viewpoint on the east side of the metro: Hood sits about 100° (ESE) roughly 58 km away, with St. Helens, Adams and Rainier to the north over Gresham and the Gorge. Go on a clear winter morning for a pink-to-gold Hood especially when low fog sits over Gresham below, or at sunset for alpenglow on Hood while the city lights come on. Park in the 20-space lot on SE Gabbert Rd by the old Brite House and walk the short, steep paved road up; only ADA parking is at the top. Peak-ID signs at the viewpoint help with St. Helens and Adams.
spots.lens: 70-300 for Hood compressed over the Gresham rooftops and for alpenglow details; 16-50 for the panorama of the Cascades over the Columbia; 27 for a clean lawn-and-mountain frame at dusk.
spots.alert: Paved loop is under half a mile; restrooms are seasonal. Check city park hours (Parks Maintenance 503-618-2525) before a pre-dawn visit.
sources: City of Gresham: Hogan Butte Nature Park
Oregon Hikers forum: Gabbert Butte and Hogan Butte (Feb 2024)

spots.name: Tsuru Island Japanese Garden (Main City Park, Gresham)
spots.tip: A small sister-city garden on an island in Main City Park, newly rebuilt in 2025–26 with a bluestone path, stone bridges, bamboo fencing, a roofed entry gate, a boulder water basin and a covered machiai bench. The arching bridge and Japanese maples are the frames. Shoot on soft overcast days in late October to November for maple color without hard shadows, or in spring bloom. The new solar lanterns and lighting are used for evening events such as the October Autumn Illumination, the one chance at a night shot.
spots.lens: 27 for natural, intimate garden frames; 16-50 for the bridge and path compositions; 70-300 to isolate maple leaves against dark foliage.
spots.alert: Open daily sunrise to sunset; admission is free. Renovation was set to finish around the end of September 2026, and the island closed at times during the work, so confirm with the Gresham Japanese Garden before going. Enter from Powell Blvd and Main St, with parking in front of the island. Photo sessions are handled through the garden's rental process.
sources: Gresham Japanese Garden: Tsuru Island renovation updates
Travel Oregon: Gresham Japanese Garden (Tsuru Island)

spots.name: Wauna Viewpoint (over Bonneville Dam)
spots.tip: Probably the best aerial view of Bonneville Dam and its two navigation locks, with Bridge of the Gods and Stevenson upriver, Table Mountain and Greenleaf Peak across the river, Hamilton Mountain and Beacon Rock to the west and Mount Adams on clear days. You look north, so the sun is behind you all day; late afternoon into sunset gives warm side-light on Table Mountain and the dam. The viewpoint is at a power-line pylon, so pick angles that keep the wires out or use them as a deliberate leading line. Time a barge in the locks for scale.
spots.lens: 70-300 for the locks, a barge or Bridge of the Gods (around 200-300 mm); 16-50 at 30-50 for the river bend with Table Mountain. The 27 is fine for the overview but you'll miss the telephoto details.
spots.alert: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass at Eagle Creek; lot fills early on weekends. 3.4 mi round trip, ~1,030 ft gain. Burned 2017 (standing dead trees), poison oak, and an active slide to cross just before the viewpoint.
sources: Oregon Hikers Field Guide: Wauna Viewpoint from Eagle Creek

spots.name: Three Corner Rock (old lookout summit)
spots.tip: A basalt pyramid on the Gorge skyline where a fire lookout once stood: concrete steps take you to within about 12 ft of the top, then a short scramble to a flat summit with a full 360. Hood and Jefferson sit to the south beyond Birkenfeld and Table Mountain, St. Helens and Rainier rise to the north and Adams to the northeast, so it works at both ends of the day: sunrise alpenglow on Hood/Jefferson, sunset side-light on St. Helens and Rainier. June adds beargrass in the meadows along the PCT. Bring a jacket; the summit gets strong wind blasts.
spots.lens: 70-300 is the main lens here: compress Hood behind the Birkenfeld/Table Mountain ridges or isolate Adams and Rainier at 200-300 mm. 16-50 at 16 for the lookout steps and rock with a volcano behind; use the 27 for a light walk-up kit only if you skip the telephoto (you shouldn't).
spots.alert: Discover Pass required. Long gravel DNR roads (CG 2000 / CG 2090) with logging trucks and unreliable cell service; carry printed directions. Limited parking for a few cars, faded signage, badly eroded old jeep track near the top, final 12 ft is a scramble.
sources: Oregon Hikers Field Guide: Three Corner Rock Hike

spots.name: Dalton Point boat ramp (river-level Gorge view)
spots.tip: One of the few places on the Oregon side where you can stand at the water's edge: Cape Horn's cliffs face you across the river to the northwest with Phoca Rock in the channel. Around early summer the sun sets toward the Cape Horn end of the river, so stay for silhouettes of the cliffs and glow on the water; calm mornings give reflections. It's usually quiet, and spring brings wildflowers along the shoreline trail. Shoreline and trail change with river level (high water in May can cut the path).
spots.lens: 16-50 for river-level foreground with Cape Horn; 70-300 to stack Cape Horn's cliffs and Phoca Rock or catch a passing barge.
spots.alert: Reachable only from I-84 westbound Exit 29 (eastbound drivers must turn around at Warrendale-Dodson). Free day-use, restrooms, rough lot. Waterfowl hunting is allowed in season; wind and barge traffic if launching a kayak.
sources: Lower Columbia Estuary Partnership: Dalton Point launch

spots.name: Oneonta Tunnel (Historic Columbia River Highway)
spots.tip: The 1914 highway tunnel through Oneonta Bluff, closed to traffic in 1948, restored for walkers and cyclists in 2009, burned in the 2017 Eagle Creek Fire and reopened in 2021. Frame the portal straight-on from the old road grade with the bluff and mossy walls around it; overcast or shade keeps contrast manageable and late-October/November maples add color. Go early: parking at the Oneonta trailhead is limited.
spots.lens: 16-50 at 16-24 for the portal and bluff; 27 for a natural through-the-tunnel view with someone walking for scale.
spots.alert: Bikes and pedestrians only. The Historic Highway east of Multnomah Falls reopened in May 2026 after viaduct work (vehicles under 35 ft). Check USFS for the status of the separate Oneonta Gorge creek walk before wading.
sources: ODOT: Historic Highway reopens east of Multnomah Falls (May 2026)
ODOT: Historic Highway news, March 2026 (Oneonta parking)

spots.name: Benson Lake & Mist Falls view
spots.region: Columbia Gorge · Benson State Recreation Area
spots.tip: Mist Falls drops about 520 ft in two plunges but can't be seen from the Historic Highway; the full view is from Benson State Recreation Area, walking west from the lake along the old road between I-84 and the large pond. It's a thin spring-fed ribbon that runs year-round but is fullest in winter and spring after rain, and the north-facing cliff is in shade most of the day, so flat overcast is ideal. Benson Lake itself gives still-water reflections of the Gorge wall on calm mornings, a quieter alternative to the Multnomah crowds next door.
spots.lens: 70-300 to isolate the falls ribbon against the cliff (100-200 mm); 16-50 for the pond and cliff with reflections. A tripod helps for slow shutter on the thin water.
spots.alert: The Benson exit off I-84 is reachable only from eastbound lanes. The scramble path to the falls base (pullout 1/4 mi west of Wahkeena) is on extremely unstable talus; not recommended.

spots.name: Blue Lake Regional Park (west shore, Mt. Hood down the lake)
spots.tip: The 61-acre lake runs almost 0.9 mi east-west, so from the west end Metro's 'Mount Hood framed by the shores of the lake' shot works: Hood at the far end over calm water, best in the still air right after the gate opens. In summer, osprey and bald eagles commute between the Columbia and the lake, and herons and turtles use the wetland and ponds north and west of the lake. In winter, look for red-tailed hawks, Canada geese and eagles. Calm, clear winter mornings give the best reflection.
spots.lens: 70-300 for Hood over the far shore and for osprey diving (fast shutter, AF-C); 16-50 at the shoreline for the full lake reflection; 27 for a quiet heron-in-the-reeds frame in the wetland.
spots.alert: Open 8 a.m. to legal sunset, closed Dec 25 and Jan 1. The vehicle fee is $5, but walk-ins and cyclists enter free. Because of the 8 a.m. gate, true sunrise is only reachable in the darkest weeks (about late Nov to Jan) unless you walk in from Marine Drive.
sources: Oregon Metro: Blue Lake Park field guide

spots.name: Chinook Landing Marine Park (entrance ponds & Columbia shore)
spots.tip: Skip the six-lane boat ramp and work the seasonal ponds by the entrance and the archery range, where Metro notes great blue herons and snowy egrets hunting and osprey fishing overhead. Low sun from either side lights the white egrets against dark water. Early morning before ramp traffic is quietest. The riverside picnic areas give open Columbia water for osprey and gull flight shots, and the Marine Drive Trail links on foot to Blue Lake about 1 km away.
spots.lens: 70-300 for egrets and herons from the pond edges (stay on the paths and let the birds settle); 16-50 for river-and-sky frames at the picnic areas.
spots.alert: Metro day-use parking is $5 per vehicle (free with the annual pass). Seasonal hours vary, so check Metro before going. Leashed pets are allowed.
sources: Oregon Metro: Boat Ramps field guide (2022)

spots.name: Troutdale Sandy River Bridge (1914 truss) from Glenn Otto Park
spots.tip: The western gateway of the Historic Columbia River Highway: a steel Pratt truss started in 1912 and opened in 1914, narrow enough for two small cars, with a wooden walkway. From the Glenn Otto Park gravel bar just upstream, frame the truss over the Sandy, with riverside fall color in late October and November. Evening light from the west rakes across the steel,; look for calm patches near the bar for a reflection. This is a different subject from Broughton's Bluff across the river (Lewis & Clark SRS).
spots.lens: 16-50 at the water's edge for the full truss and its reflection; 70-300 to compress the truss lattice or a car crossing; 27 for street-level frames from the walkway.
spots.alert: The river is swift and only a few feet deep under the bridge, so don't wade near the piers when the Sandy is high. Glenn Otto is a busy summer swim beach; shoot off-season or early.
sources: Peter Kun Frary, photographer: Columbia Gorge 30

spots.name: Edgefield (historic Multnomah County Poor Farm), Troutdale
spots.tip: The 1911 county poor farm, now on the National Register and restored by McMenamins since 1990. Its main lodge, outbuildings and grounds make an easy historic-architecture walk. The free, self-guided gardens include woodland, herb, kitchen, pond (big Gunnera leaves) and dry trough gardens, plus a pear orchard and Syrah vineyard rows that turn color in autumn. Golden-hour side light suits the brick and the vineyard rows; overcast days suit garden close-ups. A 1938 planting map of the farm hangs inside the main building.
spots.lens: 16-50 for the lodge facade and vineyard rows; 27 for detail and garden frames; 70-300 to isolate rooflines, chimneys and orchard trees.
spots.alert: This is a working hotel, restaurant and concert venue: stay on public paths, expect crowds and closures on concert nights, and ask before any staged or commercial shoot.
sources: Oregon Encyclopedia: Multnomah County Poor Farm (Edgefield)

spots.name: Salish Ponds Wetland Park (East Pond, Silver Star view)
spots.tip: Two restored gravel-pit ponds in Fairview. From the southwest side of East Pond, Silver Star Mountain sits to the northeast across the water, and calm evenings give a reflection with the summit catching late light. Winter is the season: the willow-lined shore looks its best, coots and mallards work the John Pettis Dock area, and beaver sign is common along the shore. In wet months, use the higher East Pond Trail, because the West Pond Trail often floods.
spots.lens: 16-50 for the pond and mountain reflection; 70-300 for Silver Star compressed above the far shore and for waterfowl from the dock.
spots.alert: Park at Salish Ponds Elementary (the former Reynolds HS site) or in the 10 reserved spaces off Glisan. Dogs on leash; the restroom may be locked. Trail details come from an anecdotal hiker guide, so check conditions.
sources: Oregon Hikers Field Guide: Salish Ponds Hike

spots.name: Government Island State Recreation Area (boat-in)
spots.tip: A boat-only chain of Columbia River islands, with about 15 miles of shoreline, Mt. Hood views, and wildlife including threatened Columbia white-tailed deer, wading birds, bald eagles and buffleheads. Land at Government Island Landing (west) or Bartlett Landing (east), or the north-side floating tie-up, and walk the shoreline trails on the north sides of Lemon and Government Islands. The beaches give low, clean foregrounds for Hood at sunrise and for the river at sunset. Camping below the vegetation line lets you stay for both light windows.
spots.lens: 70-300 for deer and eagles from the beach edge; 16-50 for beach-and-Hood frames; 27 for camp scenes at dusk.
spots.alert: Boat or paddle only; the nearest Metro ramp is M. James Gleason (by Broughton Beach). The interior is closed without a Port of Portland permit. No potable water, only pit toilets, fire restrictions apply, and secure your valuables. Big-river wind and boat wakes are a real hazard for paddlers.
sources: Travel Oregon: Government Island State Recreation Area
Islands.com: Columbia River island with paddle-in beach camping
